title: HTTP server
lede: Two server APIs share one engine. http.createServer((req, res) => …) is the real Node.js shape — portable to Node unchanged, currently a V1 res subset. The bespoke model where a handler returns a { status, body, headers } object is this project's own re-imagining, reachable only via the explicitly-non-Node klain:http specifier (`import http from 'klain:http'`) — it is no longer on the Node http namespace. Both run one fiber per connection on the shared select() event loop, so a slow connection never blocks the others. Everything below the two createServer rows is the klain:http model.

entries.name: http.createServer((req, res) => …)
entries.signature: http.createServer((req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse) => void).listen(port, cb?)
entries.description: The real Node.js server shape — a program written against it runs unchanged under Node. The handler gets (req, res): read request fields off req (method/url/headers), build the response by calling methods on res. Reuses the same fiber-per-connection accept loop and response writer as the bespoke path.
differences: V1 `res` subset: `res.writeHead(status[, headersObject])`/`setHeader`/`write`/`end`, the `res.statusCode` getter/setter, `res.write` returning Node's boolean and `res.cork()`/`uncork()` no-op hints, and `req.method`/`url`/`headers`. The response is buffered (flushed after the handler returns), so there is no incremental flow control: `res.write` always returns `true` and no `'drain'` fires — a large streamed response uses a `ReadableStream` `body` field instead.
The status reason phrase is hardcoded `OK` (`writeHead(201)` → `201 OK`, not `201 Created`).
One server per program, shared with the bespoke `http.listen`.

entries.name: const server = http.createServer(cb?)
entries.signature: server.listen(port?, cb?); server.close(cb?); server.address(); server.on('request'/'upgrade', cb)
entries.description: The standard Node idiom: bind to a variable, .listen(0) for an ephemeral port, read .address().port, .close() from inside the loop. The chained form const server = http.createServer(cb).listen(0, readyCb) also works — the handle is stored before the ready callback runs, so server.address().port is valid inside it.
differences: `server.listen` is **non-blocking** — it registers the listener and returns, so top-level code after it runs before requests are served (Node's listen-then-continue); the event loop drives requests from the end-of-`main` tail. The ready callback fires synchronously at `listen()` time rather than on a later tick. (The bespoke `http.listen` below stays blocking.)

`.on` supports `'request'` (one listener), `'stream'`, `'listening'`, and the Node-faithful `'upgrade'` event (`(req, socket, head)` — `socket` is a `net.Socket`, TLS-backed on an `https` server so `wss://` falls out); no `'close'`/`'error'`/`'connection'`/`'clientError'` events.

entries.name: klain:http — http.listen(port, handler)
entries.signature: import http from 'klain:http'; http.listen(port: number, handler: (req: HttpRequest) => Res): void
entries.description: This project's own server model, under the explicitly-non-Node klain:http specifier — a handler returns a { status, body, headers } object rather than writing to a res. One fiber per accepted connection (ucontext.h), so a slow connection never blocks the others, running on the shared select() event loop alongside timers, fetch, and the other socket APIs. Not on the Node http namespace: `import http from 'klain:http'`.

params.name: handler
params.desc: Returns an object with status / body / optional headers.

entries.name: http.listen(port, handler, { workers: N })
entries.description: Multi-process clustering: fork()s N-1 workers sharing the listening socket — parallelism across cores on top of each process's own fiber concurrency. cluster.isPrimary / cluster.workerId (0 = original, 1..N-1 per fork) branch on the current process. Works under both memory modes. os.cpus().length is the natural N.

entries.name: req.method / req.path
entries.description: The request line, parsed. Any method token (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/…), not GET-only. req.path excludes the query string — that's req.query.

returns.desc: The HTTP method / the path without query.

entries.name: req.headers
entries.description: Request headers as a Map. Keys are lowercased for case-insensitive lookup, matching real HTTP semantics.

entries.name: req.query
entries.description: The query string, split from req.path and parsed (a=b&c=d). Both keys and values are percent-decoded via the same decodeURIComponent primitive this compiler already had.

entries.name: req.body
entries.description: The request body as a string — Content-Length-aware, accumulated across reads, capped at 10MiB. Binary-safe: the buffer, the string value, and every string operation carry a length header, so an embedded null byte survives (an "ab\0cd" body reports length 5 and echoes 5 bytes).

entries.name: req.bodyBytes()
entries.description: Wraps the same already-buffered, Content-Length-accurate bytes into an ArrayBuffer (no copy) — an explicit ArrayBuffer view for callers that want one. req.body is itself binary-safe now, so this is a convenience rather than the only NUL-safe path.

entries.name: response headers field
entries.signature: return { status, body, headers?: Map<string, string> }
entries.description: An optional headers field on the returned response object, fully user-controlled — including Content-Type if set. Omitting the field behaves byte-identically to before it existed.

entries.name: response bodyBytes field
entries.description: An optional ArrayBuffer response body that wins outright over body's own content whenever present and non-null. The response writer writes it via an explicit-length write() (not a NUL-terminated sprintf), so a binary payload with embedded null bytes reaches the socket whole. The plain string body is itself binary-safe now, so bodyBytes is an explicit-ArrayBuffer convenience.

entries.name: streaming response body
entries.statusRow: Streaming response body (`body: ReadableStream<string \| Uint8Array>` field)
entries.description: When the returned object's body field is statically a ReadableStream, the response goes out Transfer-Encoding: chunked, written chunk-at-a-time by a promise-reaction-driven writer — the handler returns immediately and a slow producer holds only its own connection open. http.close() still waits for in-flight streams.
differences: A stream error mid-response closes the connection without the chunked terminator — nothing else is signallable mid-stream.

entries.name: req.stream()
entries.description: Streams the request body as Uint8Array chunks read off the socket. Using it switches the program to headers-complete dispatch: the handler runs once headers are parsed and the body flows as chunks (fiber-yield on EAGAIN); the 10MiB cap then applies to the header block only. Piped into a streaming response body, it echoes without ever buffering the payload.
differences: `req.body`/`req.bodyBytes()` after consuming `req.stream()` throw a catchable `TypeError` (WHATWG "body already disturbed") — though before consuming the stream they still drain the remaining body into the buffer in place and stay correct.
A handler may mix response `body` shapes across branches by declaring a union `body: string | ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` — the writer branches on the runtime tag.

entries.name: process.on('SIGINT'/'SIGTERM', handler)
entries.description: Graceful shutdown. The handler runs from ordinary control flow at the top of a loop iteration (never real signal context) and may clean up and process.exit().

entries.name: http.close()
entries.statusRow: `http.close()` (formal listener teardown, distinct from the graceful-shutdown row above)
entries.description: Formal, graceful listener teardown — a bare global function reachable only from inside a running request handler, a setTimeout/setInterval callback, or a process.on handler. Stops accepting immediately and lets already-open connections finish before http.listen()'s call returns control to the rest of the program (matching Node's default server.close()). In a { workers: N } cluster, one worker's .close() drains and exits every worker via a shared mmap'd flag, with no external signal.

entries.name: http.closeAllConnections()
entries.description: The forceful counterpart to http.close() (Node's server.closeAllConnections()): shutdown(2)s every in-flight connection so each fiber unwinds through its own EOF path. It shuts down the calling handler's own connection too (Node parity), so send the response before calling it if the response must be delivered. In a cluster, one worker's call force-closes every worker's connections via the same shared mmap flag.
